title: Harry Styles debuts emotional new song dedicated to Liam Payne
description: Harry Styles performed an unreleased song he wrote for his former One Direction bandmate Liam Payne. The Grammy Award-winning star played the track, c
body: Harry Styles performed an unreleased song he wrote for his former One Direction bandmate Liam Payne. The Grammy Award-winning star played the track, called What Is Enough, during his sold-out concert at Madison Square Garden, on the second anniversary of Payne's death. Styles is currently performing at the New York venue as part of a residency on his record-breaking Together, Together tour. Addressing the packed crowd on Friday night, the singer paid tribute to Payne as a friend and someone he "wouldn't have been able to do this without".As a spotlight shone over him, Styles made a moving speech, in which he honoured Liam Payne, who died two years ago after falling from a hotel balcony in Argentina."I feel incredibly lucky to get to play these shows here in New York, and this building means a lot to me," said the artist. "There are so many people in my life, friends and people that I've worked with that I wouldn't have been able to do this without," he continued."And two years ago today, I lost one of those friends."This was met with cheers from the audience, who were hearing What Is Enough for the first time. Wearing a royal blue jumper with a red collar, the musician then urged fans to keep an eye out for and support each other. "I'm sure a lot of you have been through similar things. I hope you haven't. "But really, it's just about looking after each other."He added that there were "so many more people who have touched my life in such special ways", thanking those who helped him get to where he is. "I'm gonna play you a song I wrote for my friend about two years ago, if that's all right."As he paused, passionate cheers and clapping could be heard from his fans.The singer then began to play his guitar and perform What is Enough, which featured emotional and reflective lyrics.As he sang out to the crowd, his band played a melodic accompaniment.Sharing their reaction to Friday night's performance on Instagram,, external Harry Styles' fans described What is Enough as "beautiful".Styles launched his solo career in 2017 after becoming a global star in One Direction.His first album and single were both UK number ones, while his record Harry's House won a Grammy and a Brit Award after its release in 2022. Listen to Newsbeat live at 12:45 and 17:45 weekdays - or listen back here.

schema.headline: Harry Styles debuts emotional new song dedicated to Liam Payne

title: Trial of German steakhouse heiress Christina Block that sparked a huge spy scandal
description: It is a trial that has gripped Germany, with a wealthy heiress in the dock for months and a case that triggered the country's biggest espionage scanda
body: It is a trial that has gripped Germany, with a wealthy heiress in the dock for months and a case that triggered the country's biggest espionage scandal in recent history.Christina Block, heir to a popular chain of steakhouses, is accused of ordering an Israeli security firm to carry out the violent abduction of her children from Denmark, following a bitter custody battle with her former husband.There are allegedly connections with at least two former secret agents, from Germany and Israel.In the latest twist, investigators in the case stumbled across evidence that has led to Germany's former intelligence chief, August Hanning, being arrested this month for treason and espionage.Hanning's arrest stunned the intelligence community. Although his case has nothing to do with the Hamburg trial, he has denied allegations of involvement in an earlier attempted abduction of the children.There was enormous media interest in Germany when Christina Block and six others went on trial in a high-security courtroom in Hamburg in July last year.Block House restaurants, specialising in steak and baked potatoes, are a feature of many German towns. Their success over the past half century has helped make Christina Block's father Eugen a multimillionaire.Prosecutors allege that she and a family lawyer, Andreas Costard, organised the forcible abduction of two of her children, who were staying with her former husband, Stephan Hensel, at his home in Denmark.They say the operation was carried out by a 36-year-old Israeli citizen named only as Jonathan G and five others.The abduction took place during the New Year celebrations of 2023-24, as the two children and their father were watching a firework display, according to the indictment.Prosecutors say several men ambushed and beat up Stephan Hensel, and dragged the boy and the girl, then 10 and 13 years old, into a car.On the approach to the border with Germany, they are alleged to have changed vehicles, taped up the children's mouths and tied the girl's hands.The group are then said to have travelled on to Baden-Württemberg in a campervan. Prosecutors say the children were held there against their will until their mother arrived to pick them up on 2 January 2024 and took them to her home in Hamburg.Christina Block, Andreas Costard and Jonathan G are charged with the abduction of minors, grievous bodily harm and unlawful detention.Block's partner, a former TV sports presenter called Gerhard Delling, and three others are charged with aiding and abetting.All of them deny wrongdoing, except for Jonathan G, who has admitted his involvement. However, he told the court he thought he was taking part in a rescue operation.The trial comes after years of legal battles between Christina Block and her former husband, Stephan Hensel, over who had the right to look after the children.Immediately after their separation, all four children lived with their mother in Hamburg. Hensel, who remarried, later moved to Denmark, where they regularly visited him.In 2021, the two youngest children went to visit their father in Denmark, but then were not brought back to Hamburg as agreed.A court in Hamburg ruled that Christina had custody and that the children should be returned. However, in February 2023, a Danish court ruled that, although the boy and the girl had been brought to Denmark unlawfully, they could not be taken back.In May 2023, Hensel was charged with the abduction of minors, in a case which is still pending.He has accused Christina of being violent with the children, charges she denies. She told the court Hensel wanted to take revenge on her.She also denied knowing anything about plans for the abduction of the children from Denmark. Her defence argues that the Israeli security team had acted on its own initiative.She told the court it was "a catastrophe" and that she had never wanted anything like that.The head of the Israeli security team, David Barkay, who is not on trial but faces future legal proceedings, told the court that Christina Block and Costard had known about the planned repatriation operation.Barkay, who was described by another witness as a former agent with Mossad, the Israeli secret service, said he had not shared all the details because he "didn't trust them."The alleged connection with Germany's former spy chief, August Hanning, relates to accusations of an earlier attempt to abduct the children and bring them back from Denmark in 2022.Prosecutors have said Hanning was responsible for arranging security staff sent to Denmark with Christina Block. His lawyer denies the accusations. Hanning has not been charged over the current Block court case.However, while investigators were searching his home, they came across evidence to suggest Hanning was involved in buying some 2,000 documents from his former chief of staff and then passing on state secrets to foreign powers. Which foreign power and who he is alleged to have given the secrets to is unspecified, but it has prompted widespread speculation.Now 80, Hanning is in custody charged with treasonous espionage. His lawyer says he is being "unjustly persecuted" and that the charges are "unfounded".Meanwhile the trial against Christina Block is currently on hold for two weeks - one of numerous delays and extensions over the course of the past 15 months.The latest delay is because a witness, Stephan Hensel's new wife, failed to appear in court.

schema.headline: Trial of German steakhouse heiress Christina Block that sparked a huge spy scandal

title: European diplomats attacked by Israeli settlers in West Bank
description: A delegation of European diplomats has been attacked by masked Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank.Belgium condemned the assault on its consul
body: A delegation of European diplomats has been attacked by masked Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank.Belgium condemned the assault on its consul general and the other envoys and called for Israel to bring those responsible to justice.The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) also condemned what they called "the severe act of violence" and said they were investigating.But the office of the Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu cast doubt on what happened and suggested it was part of a "coordinated campaign to smear Israel".The attack came only a day after a number of Palestinians and Heidi Levine, a Washington Post photographer, were injured in a separate assault by settlers in another village in the West Bank.The diplomats - from Belgium, France, Poland and the Catholic Church - had come to the largely Christian village of Taybeh near Ramallah.They were there to assess the situation on the ground after almost near daily attacks by Israeli settlers on Palestinians trying to bring in their olive harvest.Video footage from the scene showed masked settlers confronting the convoy. Reports suggest stones were thrown.The Belgian authorities said a car from its consulate had a window smashed and a French mayor was assaulted. Video showed a man wearing a French tricolor sash slumped beside a vehicle.Belgium's foreign minister Maxime Prevot condemned the attack and said Israel had a responsibility to bring those responsible to justice."Palestinians face this violence every day. Settlers also target journalists reporting on it and diplomats. Harvesting olives, reporting the news or carrying out diplomatic duties should never put anyone at risk of attack," he said. "As the occupying power, Israeli authorities must protect Palestinians, ensure the safety of diplomats and journalists, and bring those responsible to justice. "Impunity for violent settlers must end. Belgium will continue to press for EU sanctions against those responsible for this violence and those who support them."Gideon Sa'ar, Israel's foreign minister, said he strongly condemned the violence by what he called "Israeli rioters". He said the foreign ministry was in contact with the ambassadors of the countries involved.But he added: "Without detracting from the severity of the incident, it is unfortunate that the visit was not coordinated with the IDF in advance. Such coordination could have helped safeguard the visitors' security."The IDF said they "strongly condemn the severe act of violence that took place in the area of Taybeh, during which diplomatic representatives were attacked by Israeli rioters.""According to a preliminary inquiry, no IDF soldiers were present at the scene at the time of the attack," they added.But Netanyahu's office urged "caution before drawing conclusions" from reports about the attack.It said the images on social media "do not establish the complete sequence of events or individual responsibility".A statement continued: "Those circumstances remain under investigation. Israeli police and forensic investigators have launched an investigation to establish the facts and identify those responsible."It added that "these reports come amid concerns about a coordinated campaign to smear Israel and the Jewish residents of Judea and Samaria during the annual olive harvest, relying on sensational headlines before the full facts emerge".Netanyahu's office named the injured French official as Bernard Baudoux. The left-wing mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries in northern France told the AFP news agency the attack showed a tolerance by Israel's right-wing government for settler violence.The mayor said the settlers kicked him and beat him with iron bars, throwing him to the ground."It's the gratuitous nature of the violence that stuns me," he said. "They arrived completely enraged.""The whole world needs to know what's happening there. For me, I'll go back to my country and everything will be fine. Those who continue to suffer the most are those who are here," he said.

schema.headline: European diplomats attacked by Israeli settlers in West Bank

title: The Sabrina Carpenter clip that helped a 22-year-old make £120,000 a year
description: Eknoor Singh says he only needs his mobile phone and a decent internet connection to earn more than £120,000 a year.The 22-year-old Londoner is a prof
body: Eknoor Singh says he only needs his mobile phone and a decent internet connection to earn more than £120,000 a year.The 22-year-old Londoner is a professional "clipper". He is paid by clients to make short, vertical videos for social media, in the hope of them going viral."The more views a clip gets, the more money I make," he says.The way it typically works is that the client - who could be anyone from a clothing brand to a record label, movie studio, podcaster or influencer - has a longer video that the clipper watches first.He or she then makes 30 to 60-second clips of what they consider to be the best bit or bits, and uploads them to Instagram, YouTube, TikTok or other platforms.The idea is that the clippers, who are typically aged from 16 to 25, will have a better understanding of what will connect with that demographic, and get the short videos as many views as possible.For 24-year-old clipper Ethan Weems from Wichita, Kansas, it's a lucrative side hustle to his other video-making work. He says he makes "at least $1,000 a month" from clipping.He does this by making short videos for YouTuber and podcaster Caleb Hammer, who is best known for hosting a show called Financial Audit, which analyses the personal finances of his guests.Weems says clipping helps him make a living from home – giving him more time to spend with his wife and one-year-old son. "I don't want that typical nine-to-five job where I have to go into an office every day," he says.Yet while some clippers can make good money, social media consultant Lia Haberman cautions that there are very few of them. "It mirrors the creator economy more broadly. The vast majority make little to nothing," she says.Meanwhile, streaming industry analyst Devin Nash says it's easy to underestimate the time required to make clipping a success. He warns that successful clippers must "watch hours and hours of content, and they just live in that world".Connecting clippers with their prospective clients are a number of intermediary websites, where available video jobs are listed. These range from pages on general online forums such as Reddit and Discord, to dedicated clipping sites such as Clipping Culture, Vyro, Whop and Kick.The latter websites take a fee from the companies wanting the work done. Clipping Culture lists clients including Capital Records, Universal Music Group and HBO Max.For firms such as these, hiring a teenager or 20-something working from his or her bedroom is far cheaper than paying for traditional adverts on social media, and likely to be more effective in terms of getting eyeballs.That's the experience of Boxabl, a Las Vegas-based firm that makes modular homes. "I think we've done probably a billion views [of clips] so far," says founder Galiano Tiramani, who features in many of the company's videos.In the UK, Jimmy McLoughlin, a former Downing Street adviser and now host of the Jimmy's Jobs of the Future podcast, has also embraced clips."The clips are almost like trailers for the main events," he says. For instance, a recent podcast with Prime Minister Andy Burnham "had close to 50,000 long plays, but in terms of clips, it's done millions".

schema.headline: The Sabrina Carpenter clip that helped a 22-year-old make £120,000 a year

title: Pope discharged from hospital days after lung cancer surgery
description: Pope Leo XIV has been discharged from Rome's Gemelli Hospital, just four days after an operation to remove a cancerous growth from his lung.The 71-yea
body: Pope Leo XIV has been discharged from Rome's Gemelli Hospital, just four days after an operation to remove a cancerous growth from his lung.The 71-year-old walked unaided to his waiting car, stopping to speak to well-wishers.The Vatican said the Pope will give the traditional Angelus prayer and blessing to a crowd in St Peter's Square on Sunday, as he did last week when he surprised the world by announcing the surgery.On Friday, photographs were released of the Pope celebrating Mass and distributing communion in hospital for staff. A statement from his doctors said blood tests and a chest X-ray showed "steady improvement" following his operation.The surgery on Tuesday, which lasted for 90 minutes, included the removal of the lower lobe of the Pope's right lung. The results of further tests to check for any sign that the cancer has spread have not yet been announced.The Pope also spoke to Russian President Vladimir Putin on Friday, in their first call since June 2025. The Vatican said the call was to urge "dialogue and peace".It came as Russia's bombardment of cities across Ukraine intensifies, with a growing number of civilian casualties and no sign of Putin being ready to halt the invasion.The Pope also called for a humanitarian ceasefire in the Ukrainian city of Oleshkiy, occupied by Russia and under constant shelling, to allow people to be evacuated and for the urgent delivery of food and medicine. The BBC recently reported on residents there being forced to eat garden weeds to survive.The Pope's schedule has been cleared completely until 20 October, so his reappearance in public so soon is a surprise and will be some relief for Catholics around the world.Those close to the Pope said he was keen not to delay a trip to Latin America, planned for early November and which includes a visit to Peru, where he was a missionary for many years.It is not yet clear whether he might be fit to travel or require further treatment.

schema.headline: Pope discharged from hospital days after lung cancer surgery

title: France protests: Violent clashes, looting and buildings ablaze as over 1,000 arrested
description: Figure caption, How day of protests unfolded as disorder breaks out across FranceByJack BurgessUpdated 1 hour agoViolence broke out across France on S
body: Figure caption, How day of protests unfolded as disorder breaks out across FranceByJack BurgessUpdated 1 hour agoViolence broke out across France on Saturday during the latest day of demonstrations against education standards and the cost of living.At least 1,200 people were arrested during what the French government described as an "escalation in violence" alongside an estimated 550,000 taking to the streets.In Paris, there were significant clashes into the evening with riot police, who used tear gas and water cannon on crowds. Buildings were set alight in the capital and other areas, including in Limoges where a large fire in the town hall caused the roof to partly collapse.Looting broke out in several cities, with widespread vandalism targeted against city halls and businesses also reported.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, La Barrique bar in Paris was set on fireSixty law enforcement officers were injured, including two who were taken to hospital unconscious, France's Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said.In Paris, the main march appeared to be largely peaceful during the afternoon. A group of young people told the BBC they were "pacifists" who are "just trying to make things change, but nothing is moving".However, as the day wore on some groups lit fires in the street and torched vehicles, including in iconic locations in the city centre like the Place de la République.Shops were ransacked, at least one restaurant was gutted by fire, and the BBC saw fighting breaking out among some of the groups.Riot police were seen charging at one crowd in central Paris and hitting several people with batons.Image source, ReutersImage caption, A car was set alight at the Place de la République in ParisIn Lyon, Mayor Grégory Doucet said the burning of the city's tourist office was "a tragedy" for the city, telling BFMTV "it breaks our hearts because it's a very iconic, well-known historic building".Local police said "hostile individuals" prevented firefighters from safely tackling the blaze.Fire crews also battled the fire at Limoges town hall, which the local prefecture said caused part of the building to collapse.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Limoges town hall was "largely lost" in a blaze, the prefecture saidA young man "had his hand blown off by a grenade" in Saint-Étienne, the south-eastern city's Mayor Régis Juanico said on social media, adding: "Such a tragedy should never have happened."The interior ministry said the protests involved "targeted acts of violence" from "hooded individuals" in places, including parts of the capital and also Marseille, Rennes, Toulouse and Angers.Damage to buildings was reported across France, including in Grenoble, Avignon, Pau, Montpellier and Valence.Clothes and food shops were raided in Paris, while an Apple store in Lille was broken into and emptied.Footage authenticated by BBC Verify showed a tourist train in Grenoble being driven by masked men along a narrow street in the city centre towards at least three riot police officers.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Rapid-response riot police were deployed in Paris Hundreds of thousands of students have protested in recent weeks over staff shortages and dilapidated facilities in the country's lycées - secondary schools attended by 15 to 18-year-olds.On Saturday, their numbers were bolstered by trade union members and other protest groups. These groups include the so-called gilets jaunes 'yellow vest' movement, who demonstrated against cost-of-living hikes for over a year from 2018 - becoming one of the longest-lived protest movements in French history.While France is no stranger to outbreaks of protest and disorder, this round comes as the country heads into a period of deep political uncertainty.French President Emmanuel Macron will leave office next year and polls suggest April's presidential election could come down to a fight between the leader of the National Rally, Marine Le Pen, and Jean-Luc Mélenchon of the hard-left La France Insoumise party.The latter took part in demonstrations in France and later accused police officers of "unleashing" on protesters, while condemning looting and arson.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Shops were looted in Paris, and other cities, during demonstrations on SaturdayFigure caption, Watch: 'The mood has really shifted' at the Paris student protestsFrance's Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said his comments were "dangerous and cynical".He earlier said police had faced "violence of extreme intensity" and some groups were using the protests as a "warm-up" for the presidential elections, adding: "No-one will impose their political agenda through violence."Le Pen said "legitimate demands" voiced by protesters had been "held hostage by the far left", accusing Mélenchon of fuelling the violence.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Police fired water cannon at protesters in the Place de la République, ParisFrench President Emmanuel Macron said: "Those who have broken, attacked the prefectures as well as businesses, looted even our town halls, will be prosecuted and punished."The government has made apparent attempts at concessions, with Education Minister Édouard Geffray promising 3,000 extra supply teachers, during a television interview on 8 October.However, the protests have continued and intensified.

schema.headline: France protests: Violent clashes, looting and buildings ablaze as over 1,000 arrested

title: Trump waives several Russia sanctions as row with Zelensky intensifies
description: Donald Trump blocked numerous sanctions on Russia two days before they were due to take effect, as a row with his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zele
body: Donald Trump blocked numerous sanctions on Russia two days before they were due to take effect, as a row with his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky deepens.The sanctions were passed by the Congress and signed into law the president in September.But Trump issued an executive order Friday night saying that suspending some was in the US national interest, prompting a backlash from US lawmakers. Zelensky said it was unfortunate the US has decided to "completely disregard" the sanctions.Relations between Washington and Kyiv frayed after the US struck a controversial deal to import Russian diesel last week. Ukraine has accused the Trump administration of withdrawing key military support.Trump and Zelensky have exchanged sharp words about one another. Ukraine's president declared it was nice to be among "real leaders" while addressing an EU summit, after Trump said Zelensky was "more difficult to deal with" than Russian President Vladimir Putin.The new US sanctions law took aim at Russia's economy by giving Trump broad powers to levy tariffs of up to 100% on imports from the top five purchasers of Russian oil and gas – most significantly China and India.It also included sanctions against senior Russian figures, including Putin, as well as Russian financial institutions and Moscow's so-called "shadow fleet" of vessels used to circumvent existing embargoes.Many of these provisions have now been waived by Trump.Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev called the waiver "an important and truly historic moment".Posting on X, he said the sanctions would have inflicted "serious damage", primarily on the US and global market, and that economic cooperation benefits both nations.Democrats including the Virginia Congressman Don Beyer criticised the move, accusing Trump of capitulating to Moscow and turning his back on Kyiv and Zelensky. "Trump's latest surrender to Putin again betrays our Ukrainian partners and defies clear congressional intent of legislation designed to punish Russia for its illegal war of aggression," Beyer wrote on X. A handful of Republicans, too, have come out against the move.Senator Ted Cruz of Texas, a Trump ally, called waving sanctions against Russia a mistake, saying on Fox News: "I wish the president hadn't done it."He added there were other ways to could address diesel prices and "the current path, unfortunately, just... benefits Putin and that's not a good idea."Senator John Cornyn, also of Texas, said on X: "Helping Putin in Ukraine is reckless. He would not stop with Ukraine and our NATO allies would be next."North Carolina Senator Thom Tillis called it "beyond irresponsible", noting the sanctions legislation passed the chamber with bipartisan support and a large majority - only 11 senators voted against it. Trump could bring down energy prices "by solving the Iran problem, not by doing a solid for Vladimir Putin," he said.Nebraska Representative Don Bacon said many lawmakers will resist funding the president's agenda "knowing he is propping up a dictator's invasion and throwing an ally under the bus".The move is likely to draw further anger from Ukraine, where Zelensky has long stressed the need for stringent sanctions to limit funding Russia can use in its war effort.Zelensky said on Saturday morning that the sanctions "could have helped enormously" and that the law was "supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia to bring this war to an end".He pointed to Russian overnight attacks on 15 Ukrainian energy facilities that had caused power cuts in several regions and said: "Russia is trying to cause a blackout in Ukraine – right before winter."Zelensky said it was "important that everyone in America also sees what is really happening" on the ground.He later told reporters that he believed the Trump administration would lift more sanctions against Russia.Negotiators from Ukraine spoke to their US counterparts on Friday and that both teams could meet next week, he also said.Trump was initially criticised by Zelensky and Ukraine's European allies for temporarily suspending some US sanctions to import Russian diesel in a bid to bring down US energy prices, which have skyrocketed during the Iran war. His Republican party is at risk of losing control of the US Congress, in next month's midterm elections, largely due to voters' sour mood about affordability.Zelensky suggested the deal was tantamount to the US investing in Russia's war effort.A few days later, Trump claimed that both Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an "energy ceasefire" to facilitate the export of Russian diesel. Both nations have been intensively striking one another's energy infrastructure. Kyiv says this is to limit revenue for Russia's war machine, while Moscow claims it only targets facilities used by the Ukrainian military.Zelensky initially expressed surprise at Trump's announcement, and said Kyiv would stop the strikes if Russia did the same. After three days of fresh attacks from Russia, Kyiv resumed its strikes on Russian oil refineries.Trump, condemned Ukraine's strikes as a disgrace, but Zelensky said he was "only standing up for Ukraine's interests". Concerns that Trump is siding with Russia have been heightened by disruption to a US-provided satellite system used by Ukraine.  Last week Starlink suddenly and unexpectedly restricted the speed at which drones could fly while still maintaining internet connection. This disrupted some battlefield missions, Ukraine said, and hampered Kyiv's ability to protect itself from incoming Russian attacks. During the slowdown, Russia launched several deadly strikes on Ukraine, with residents and the government saying these came with no prior warning.Zelensky told reporters on Saturday that Ukraine had been told by US officials the speed restrictions were linked to technical issues.However, he said Ukraine had tested Starlink on EU territory and found "these problems do not exist" and the system was operating at higher speeds.Trump has denied halting intelligence-sharing and deliberately slowing down the network.Ukrainian authorities have confirmed that at least nine people have been killed and around 60 injured in Russian strikes across the country over the past 24 hours. That included an ambulance driver killed and 20 others injured in a Russian strike on the city of Kherson, they said.Russia's defence ministry said it had targeted industries linked to Ukraine's defence industry - including steel works, an electrical sub-station and a cargo vessel in the Black Sea.Additional reporting by Helen Sullivan and Sareen Habeshian

schema.headline: Trump waives several Russia sanctions as row with Zelensky intensifies

title: Man City 3-2 Ipswich: Boos and bananas on day of defiance at Etihad Stadium
description: Figure caption, Haaland nets double as Man City go six points clear at the topByNeil JohnstonBBC Sport football reporterIt started with Manchester Cit
body: Figure caption, Haaland nets double as Man City go six points clear at the topByNeil JohnstonBBC Sport football reporterIt started with Manchester City supporters booing the Premier League anthem and ended with Phil Foden taking an inflatable banana into his Match of the Day interview after helping see off Ipswich to pull six points clear at the top of the table.On a day of defiance in east Manchester, City's fans made their feelings crystal clear in their first top-flight home game since being found guilty of breaching Premier League financial rules.Tens of thousands inside Etihad Stadium booed and jeered when the Premier League anthem was played over the speakers shortly before kick-off, then they started chanting 'City, City, City'.The anger did not last.There was a chant about playing Stockport away and the gallows humour continued when City fans sang 'You're going down with the City' to Ipswich's travelling support.City boss Enzo Maresca, who is the first manager in Premier League history to win his first seven games in charge, said afterwards he felt the air of defiance from the stands even before kick-off."The environment was very good," said the Italian after a game watched by 60,817, a new record crowd at Etihad Stadium."The fans, the club and the players are all together on this journey."Figure caption, Manchester City manager Maresca reacts to win against Ipswich TownCity fans go bananasCity fans arrived at the ground to find hundreds of inflatable bananas had been placed on seats in the home sections for fans to wave throughout the game.They were visible in the away end at Liverpool last week but this was on a different scale and the Etihad was turned into a sea of yellow.The inflatables are a flashback to the late '80s when what began as a light-hearted joke soon turned into one of the most memorable fan crazes in English football.They are enjoying a revival at a time when City have appealed after being found guilty of charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial rules between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons, and creating 'sham contracts' to inflate sponsorship deals by £830m.There were surreal scenes at one point on Saturday as fans jeered during the Premier League anthem while waving the inflatables in the air."You can tell they are behind us and they're pushing us," Phil Foden said when asked about the fans after scoring on his return to the side following suspension after being sent off against Manchester United on 13 September.Foden's 19th-minute opener was his first goal of 2026."It's nice to play at home and you can hear how loud they are," he added. "They're giving us that extra boost that we need."Figure caption, Phil Foden goes bananas!'I didn't expect to win seven out of seven'Taking over from Pep Guardiola - 20 trophies during 10 seasons in charge - was always going to be a big challenge for Maresca.Seven matches in, City's Premier League record remains flawless.No points dropped, seven wins out of seven despite falling behind against Bournemouth and playing for more than an hour with 10 men at Manchester United."For sure I didn't expect to win seven out of seven," said Maresca. "We are working well and working good. "I'm very happy especially with the situation in general."Today we controlled the game for 95 minutes. We created chances, we scored. "We finished with a little bit of suffering together but overall, it is good."On Foden's impressive return to action, Maresca added: "I said since day one that I love Phil. I know him from years ago and I know how good he is. "It's a matter of helping him to again be one of the best players in the Premier League."'I give my players credit'Despite the off-field turmoil, this is City's best start to a league season in 129 years.Only Chelsea in 2005-06 (first nine) and Liverpool in 2019-20 (first eight) have ever won the first seven matches of a Premier League campaign.Both went on to win the title."First of all, I am very happy because it's a matter of winning games in this business," said Maresca after the game."We were able to win seven in a row and what made me very happy was day by day with the players, the way they are working and how I can see them improving."Today I thought we controlled the game, created chances and [were] good off the ball. We are doing well and I think that's the most important thing."On his players dealing with the events surrounding the club off the field, Maresca said: "They are not worried about people who judge from outside because they know people are trying to judge them."Inside, I promise the players are happy. They're getting credit and I give credit to them."Follow Manchester City on BBC SoundsPre-match, post-match and topical City contentSubscribe and listen for everything you love about City

schema.headline: Man City 3-2 Ipswich: Boos and bananas on day of defiance at Etihad Stadium

title: Isle of Wight fossil identified as new dinosaur species
description: Image source, Sergey Krasovskiy and Pedro SalasImage caption, Invictibellatrix amberina is thought to have lived in the Early Cretaceous period about
body: Image source, Sergey Krasovskiy and Pedro SalasImage caption, Invictibellatrix amberina is thought to have lived in the Early Cretaceous period about 120 million years agoA new species of dinosaur - a long-clawed predator the size of a large tiger - has been identified from a fossil found on the Isle of Wight more than 100 years ago.The dinosaur, named Invictibellatrix amberina, is described in a new paper in the journal Royal Society Open Science and belongs to a group of agile, two-legged carnivores called megaraptorans.Megaraptorans were closely related to tyrannosaurs including Tyrannosaurus rex but had slender heads and attacked prey with their large arms and giant curved claws instead of their jaws.Dr Cassius Morrison of University College London (UCL) said it was a "real mystery" why the fossil - a chunk of the back of a skull - had been overlooked in the Natural History Museum.The fossil was originally found at the foot of a cliff on the south-west coast of the Isle of Wight by amateur palaeontologist Reginald Walter Tooley and was acquired by the Natural History Museum in 1924.Invictibellatrix, meaning "unconquered female warrior", is one of the smallest and earliest of the group to be found, living in the Early Cretaceous period about 120 million years ago.Image source, Trustees of the Natural History MuseumImage caption, The researchers undertook a CT scan of the fossilResearchers believe Invictibellatrix would have been three to four metres long and just over a metre and a half in height - about as tall as a human.It would likely have had feathers and its claws might have been about 10cm to 20cm long.It would have eaten small dinosaurs, lizards and mammals – occupying a similar role in the food chain to the hyena today.Megaraptors are regarded as the most mysterious of the large, meat-eating dinosaurs, as few megaraptor fossils have been found.Until now no megaraptorans had been found in Europe.Lead author Dr Cassius Morrison (UCL Earth Sciences) said: "It is a real mystery that this fossil was overlooked for so long, sitting in a drawer for nearly 100 years. "Lots of bones are found on the Isle of Wight – who knows what else is waiting to be discovered."The researchers undertook a CT scan of the fossil, creating a 3D model of this part of the skull.They compared the fossil with skulls and brain cases from tyrannosaurs, spinosaurs, raptors and other two-legged meat-eating dinosaurs.Image caption, Cliffs on the Isle of Wight are hotspots for fossil discoveriesThe research team also used mathematical modelling to investigate how the spread of megaraptors around the world might have changed over time, based on fossils discovered so far, dinosaurs' evolutionary trees, geography and climate.It was one of more than 1,000 specimens discovered by Tooley that were acquired by the Natural History Museum after his death.Professor Paul Barrett, the study's senior author from the Natural History Museum, said: "Despite over 200 years of collecting, the Isle of Wight continues to surprise us with new dinosaur species."Work like this shows the exceptional value of working with historical museum collections where there are still many discoveries to be made."The study did not explain why megaraptors likely died out in the north, but this may have been a result of shifts in climate or environment, or the presence of competing predators such as other tyrannosaurs.Get in touchYour Voice

schema.headline: Isle of Wight fossil identified as new dinosaur species

title: Social media algorithms: What if you could turn them off?
description: Toxic algorithms wouldn't let them go - now Australia wants an off switchFigure caption, Watch: Many social platforms already have following-only feed
body: Toxic algorithms wouldn't let them go - now Australia wants an off switchFigure caption, Watch: Many social platforms already have following-only feeds - here's how they workByTiffanie TurnbullSydneyWarning: This article contains an account of living with an eating disorderVarsha Yajman was already self-conscious about the way she looked when she joined social media as a 13-year-old.Endless workout videos making impossible promises filled her feeds. Through the screen, girls she'd never met urged her to sign up to dangerous calorie challenges. Others proudly promoted their height and weight - even the number of times they had been sent to hospital - on their profiles in a form of twisted competition.Every night as she fell asleep, Varsha would watch a stranger on the internet diarising what they'd consumed that day."I was like, 'I don't need to eat. I can just watch other people eat'," Varsha tells the BBC."I would find that I'd be down these really deep rabbit holes... it was like no matter how hard you tried to get out, you couldn't."Now 24 and in recovery from anorexia, Varsha says she is still served weight loss content on social media - despite having every safety setting turned on, and an exhaustive list of banned words.Image source, Tiffanie Turnbull / BBCImage caption, Varsha Yajman says social media aggravated her eating disorderIt is people like her the Australian government says it is trying to protect with a new suite of laws cracking down on big tech, which were introduced to parliament this week.The centrepiece of their proposed reforms: an algorithm switch which would force social media platforms to let users turn off recommender content. The idea is that you would only see posts from accounts you follow.It isn't the first government to try this, but existing algorithm controls are often transient and come with trade-offs in app functionality.Australia has set out to make its legislation tighter to stop this. And it hopes its new laws – which would also impose a legal duty of care on online services – will help Australians become happier and healthier.But critics are concerned Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's government has bitten off more than it can chew in its fight with big tech, while others, including the Trump administration, say the reforms threaten free speech.The choiceFlynn Martin knows what it is like to be sucked into an algorithmic spiral.Self-proclaimed misogynist influencer Andrew Tate and other manosphere figures started overwhelming the then-20-year-old's social media feeds about four years ago.It was a time when Flynn, who was eventually diagnosed with bipolar disorder, was insecure, frustrated with his life and struggling with his mental health. He says he fell for the rhetoric.He soon went viral in Australia for two videos: one ranting about whether it was OK to be a straight white male, and another where he criticised a date for her frozen yoghurt order."You find yourself in like a bit of an echo chamber... It's easy to get swept up in that," he tells the BBC."I really bought into the idea we were living in this matrix, we had this really negative system that was designed against you. And the only way to break out of it was becoming this alpha male character."The Melbournian was only pulled from the manosphere after a period of psychosis and a hospital stay.Image source, Daniel Fermer / ABC NewsImage caption, Flynn Martin says he's still finding a healthy balance with social mediaNowadays, he finds it tough to look back at that version of himself: "While there's a bit of shame and embarrassment... I think there is a bit of empathy for that younger man."Both Flynn and Varsha know social media alone isn't to blame for the worst chapter of their lives, but say it was a key factor.Countless others have stories of being confronted by social media content they didn't seek out, and didn't want to see – and there's long been suspicions the algorithms curating these platforms are harming users.Social media firms argue the potential risks are being overstated and that they already provide users with effective safety tools.But research emerging from around the world has been sketching a different picture.Studies have found social media use triggers a similar brain response to gambling and substance addiction, external; that algorithms – often unsolicited – serve up content which harms users' mental health, external, and that they're spreading disinformation and increasing polarisation, driving violence offline.Court cases and whistleblowers have aired claims that these companies know the dangers and are willing to overlook them as this technology lifts user engagement and their bottom line."The result is that they promote content that is outrageous or that invokes strong emotions from people - so it might be anger or fear or desire or lust or insecurity, whatever it is, it's going to keep us scrolling," Chanel Contos tells the BBC.Image source, Cordelia Hsu/ReutersImage caption, Consent education campaigner Chanel Contos lobbied the government for change after founding the Teach Us Consent website in 2021While studying the topic at university, the activist - who helped reform sexual consent education standards in Australia - came up with a campaign for change."Fix Our Feeds" demanded recommended algorithms be turned off by default, and social media users be given the choice to opt into them.Contos envisaged a nostalgic return to the social media of the early 2010s – a time when a person's social media was filled with posts from friends or people they actually followed and their feeds were finite.More than 15,000 people signed her petition, and the campaign also won the backing of two former prime ministers, several MPs, influential figures, mental health advocates, and online safety experts.The government in September said it had listened to the Australians who had backed Contos's campaign, and announced a version of her proposal: forcing big tech to introduce an algorithm switch - but stopping short of requiring it be automatically set to off."This is not about giving government control, it is about giving people control," Albanese said."If people want to doom scroll… that's fine, that's up to them."Image source, Hilary Wardhaugh/Getty ImagesImage caption, Communications Minister Anika Wells (left podium) and Australian PM Anthony Albanese (right podium) announcing the upcoming Digital Duty of Care bill The policy is part of the government's Digital Duty of Care bill, which would require online services – social media firms, gaming sites, chatbots and more – to "ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, a safe online environment".Children must be protected from "harmful" material and design features – for example, pornography and material which encourages eating disorders or harmful attitudes towards women – and adults must be protected from "seriously harmful" material and conduct, a much narrower list of illegal content. Breaches of the law could attract fines of up A$100m (£52m, $70m)."The digital duty of care answers a lot of the 'what abouts' of the social media minimum age law because it's much broader; it captures all online services and it shifts the onus of responsibility from the shoulders of victims onto the shoulders of the big tech operators who seek to make money off Australian users," Communications Minister Anika Wells told the BBC.The challengesThere's been a muted response from big tech. Meta, Snap, TikTok, X and Google, which owns YouTube, have all declined BBC requests for comment, and have not made public statements about the legislation.In the days after the announcement, Instagram boss Adam Mosseri argued non-algorithmic feeds would mean users saw fewer posts from friends, and said he didn't believe his app was addictive – although a US jury recently ruled otherwise."I think we conflate the way we colloquially use the word 'addicted' – like, 'I'm addicted to this show, and I'm binge-watching it' – and clinical addiction," he told a press briefing in Sydney.Image source, Jason Henry/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesImage caption, Instagram chief Adam Mosseri argues recommender algorithms are essential to user enjoymentRight-wing parties in Australia – and the Trump administration – have said the algorithms proposal and the broader bill both risk forcing over-moderation and censorship.But those who defend the law say that won't happen because you can still follow who you want and share what you want. "If adults listen to manosphere podcasts, or people post their views about the government, or make memes, or want to say the moon landing was fake – they can continue to do so without restriction," Wells said this week.The proposal seems to be far less divisive amongst the public and online safety experts compared with Australia's social media ban for children.However, the big question is: how will Australia implement this policy when, so far, it has been struggling to implement the ban? Surveys suggest most children who were on social media before the ban still are, and no fines have been issued.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Australian regulators are investigating potential breaches of the social media banThe EU's attempt at introducing algorithm controls in 2023 – after which platforms rolled out following-only feeds – is a cautionary tale.Social media firms have indicated the take-up of safety and control features like this has been low and cite it as evidence users like their products the way they are. Experts say there is a reason for that."Platforms do what the law orders, but in such a clunky way that users don't actually enjoy the option and stick with the default, algorithmic experience," researcher Chris Zomer, from the ARC Centre of Excellence for the Digital Child, wrote in The Conversation, external.On Instagram for example, when you turn off the algorithm, you can't see direct messages or access your profile and settings. When you leave the app, it reverts back to an algorithm-governed feed on your return.The only place where these issues don't exist is the Netherlands. It was changed there after a Dutch court last year found Meta in breach of the EU's Digital Services Act.Image source, Benjamin Fanjoy/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesImage caption, Meta lost an appeal against the Dutch court's ruling in March, meaning users in the Netherlands retain choice over their home feedsThe rules for Australia aren't set in stone yet, but the government says following-only feeds must not be harder to use or less functional, that algorithm settings must be "obvious", and that they must not change without an "explicit choice" by the user, even if they leave the app.Buoyed by her success in Australia, Contos is now taking her campaign global."We feel like Canada, UK, Australia are all very aligned on online safety... Then if those three jurisdictions are doing it, it could become a critical mass thing."Though experiences like theirs helped inspire these reforms, both Flynn and Varsha are somewhat sceptical of them.Varsha says she struggles to believe a country like Australia can outmuscle big tech: so she's not sure the Digital Duty of Care bill will work. And Flynn says lawmakers should be "realistic" about the potential of the algorithm switch: "At the end of the day we use social media as a form of entertainment."Polling earlier this month indicated two-thirds of their fellow Gen-Zs would keep their social media algorithms – though nearly half of Australians more generally would turn theirs off.Though Varsha admits she is unlikely to make much use of an algorithm switch, she appreciates having the choice."On a bad day I'm still susceptible to all of the things that I was at 17. To know that, if I'm having a bad day, I can opt out makes me feel really good."If you've been affected by the issues raised in this story, you could speak to a health professional or an organisation that offers support. Details of organisations offering advice and support for people in the UK are available from BBC Action Line.

schema.headline: Social media algorithms: What if you could turn them off?

title: Halloween costumes 2026: From Obsession to Odyssey, the top TV, film and pop culture party outfits

body: The whimsical fashion trend, which has dominated social media feeds in 2026, is also predicted to be a big influence this Halloween for women. Think gargoyles, moths, mushrooms, woodland fairies and 17th Century Pierrot clowns.In keeping with the theme, Lauren Sidebottom, a TikTok beauty and fashion creator from Leeds, is planning on dressing up as a weeping angel.The 23-year-old, who studied theatrical makeup at college, says she'll be creating the look using body paint, grey tights, a cracking makeup effect on her skin, drawn-on tears, and a grey wig.Women her age are, she says "wanting to look cool, different, not like every other girl," with their whimsical costumes.Tiggy Bellinger, 21, from West Sussex, agrees DIY costumes can help avoid people wearing "the exact same thing".

title: DIY SOS to be 'rested' next year to save money, BBC says
description: The long-running home renovation TV series DIY SOS will be "rested" next year in the light of "savings challenges", the BBC has said.It will be replac
body: The long-running home renovation TV series DIY SOS will be "rested" next year in the light of "savings challenges", the BBC has said.It will be replaced by a spin-off show featuring highlights from past episodes. Sources denied reports in the Sun newspaper the programme would be axed as part of a plan to make savings. Presented by Nick Knowles, DIY SOS sees a team transform the homes of families who are facing severe illness, disability, bereavement or building disasters.It was first broadcast in 1999 and is currently airing its 35th series on BBC One and iPlayer.The decision comes during the corporation's drive to save £500m over three years. It has already cancelled several well-known TV shows including Blankety Blank, Celebrity Mastermind and Live At The Apollo.A BBC spokesperson said: "In light of the BBC's savings challenges we have taken the decision to rest DIY SOS in 2027 and commission a new spin-off show instead from producers South Shore."DIY SOS Rebuilt My Life will revisit successes from the show's past and expand the brand on the BBC in a more cost-effective way next year."

schema.headline: DIY SOS to be 'rested' next year to save money, BBC says

title: Anti-government protesters battle with police in Albania
description: Figure caption, Watch: The BBC reports from Tirana, where violent protests grew on SaturdayByNick ThorpeCorrespondentReporting fromTirana, AlbaniaDemo
body: Figure caption, Watch: The BBC reports from Tirana, where violent protests grew on SaturdayByNick ThorpeCorrespondentReporting fromTirana, AlbaniaDemonstrators and riot police fought pitched battles in the centre of Tirana on Saturday for the fifth day in a row. Masked protesters, many of them high school and university students, hurled rocks and petrol bombs at riot police trying to defend the education ministry, one of the focal points of the protests. The police responded with water cannon and volleys of tear gas, sending the crowds scattering. There are also reports that rubber bullets were used for the first time.Protests which began in the summer have grown into a wider anti-government movement, with calls for the prime minister to resign following corruption allegations linked to his administration.Many of the protesters in central Tirana wore gas masks or face masks, while volunteers handed out syringes of saline eyewash to reduce the pain from the tear gas which billows down the street.The constant boom of petrol bombs could be heard exploding on Saturday.During the afternoon, the focus of the protests shifted to the office of Prime Minister Edi Rama on the city's main boulevard. Here the crowds swelled to far larger numbers than on previous days. Riot police faced a steady hail of cobble stones and fireworks, and responded with barrage after barrage of tear gas, some of the canisters landing far back in the crowds, causing panic. Incensed by the gas, the crowds waited for it to clear, then renewed their attacks.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Demonstrators come equipped to clean tear gas from people's eyesBlack smoke from a burning vehicle and the sirens of police cars and ambulances split the afternoon. As dusk fell, police special forces arrived to reinforce the riot police. Many people have been injured on both sides, 80 people have been charged with disorder so far, and hundreds more have been arrested, or are under investigation.The centre of the Tirana looks increasingly like a war zone, scattered with broken glass and burnt debris.George, a 19-year-old medical student who works as an electrician to fund his studies, stood near the burnt-out education ministry building, a scarf wrapped round his face and goggles covering his eyes. He is one of the thousands who have taken part in the increasingly intense protests which began in early June.In his gloved hands he clutched two rocks intended for the police.Asked if he was concerned about injuring them, he said: "We have mothers too. We have family too."We were peaceful for 135 days. Now we are trying to do like in France… we are trying to make a revolution. "Our government doesn't want peace, so we are using violence."Image caption, Klodi, 21 and Klea, 17, were among the young student protesters in Tirana on Saturday Many of the protesters were even younger. Klea, 17, is in her first year of university in Tirana. She said: "All the students are boycotting their university classes and left school to fight for our rights." She alleged there were provocateurs among the protesters, smashing up stores and banks, to discredit the demonstrations.Image caption, Protesters and riot police fought running battles throughout the day in the centre of the capital Socialist Party Prime Minister Edi Rama has been in power for 13 years and has dominated Albanian politics, much like his main rival Sali Berisha, of the opposition Democratic Party, did for decades. The students say they are against "the whole corrupt political class". So what is the alternative?Osman Stafa, a prominent journalist for the News24 channel, who also describes himself as an activist for change, called for a "neutral, caretaker government for one year, to organise new elections".The irony for the wider European community during this latest wave of unrest is that Rama has long been viewed favourably by the EU, which Albania aspires to join.In a social media post on Saturday morning, he urged Albanian to "not forget that we have achieved extraordinary things".He blamed the protests on the opposition Democratic Party, and on what he called "the sinister agenda of foreign actors, intent on halting our progress" towards EU membership, which he has promised by 2030. He did not name which "foreign actors" he had in mind.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Protesters threw bricks at police on the city's main boulevard The latest protests have seriously tarnished Rama's carefully cultivated image as a charming leader, steering his country towards prosperity. Parallel to the protests, a series of investigations by the special prosecution service also threaten his rule. Set up under EU and US pressure in 2019, the prosecutors recently arrested the powerful secret service chief Vlora Hyseni. She stands accused of helping a prominent businessman, former government official, and personal friend of Rama, Ergys Agasi, evade justice. The 39-year-old is under arrest. Agasi, speaking through his lawyer, denied the allegations against him and said he had nothing to do with corruption. Hyseni told prosecutors that she contacted Agasi to try to recruit him to the intelligence services.Several Albanian media outlets claim he acted as an intermediary between the prime minister and organised criminal groups. Rama has admitted that he knows Agasi but denies any knowledge of illegal transactions."Edi Rama is caught between a rock and a hard place," Lutfi Dervishi, a political analyst and university lecturer, told the BBC. "He's the victim of his own success. By concentrating so much power in his own hands, he has made himself the only person the people blame for their grievances."Rama's Socialist Party has a comfortable majority, with 83 out of 140 seats in the Albanian Parliament. The next parliamentary elections are not due till 2029.

title: Swinney's emotional explanation for his commitment to independence
description: Figure caption, John Swinney said son is 'reason' for independenceByScotland political editorThis was a more emotional speech than we are used to from
body: Figure caption, John Swinney said son is 'reason' for independenceByScotland political editorThis was a more emotional speech than we are used to from John Swinney. His voice quivered as he explained that his personal commitment to the cause is for the future of his 15-year-old son, Matthew.Then the autocue stalled and the SNP leader is heard saying under his breath "oh, come on".A period of silence was broken by the conference crowd who came to his rescue with a standing ovation.Without the prime minister's name being mentioned, this section of the speech seemed to be a response to Andy Burnham's emotional appeal for the union in memory of his father at the Labour conference in Liverpool.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Andy Burnham has called for greater devolution in Scotland earlier this weekThere was a more obvious dig at the prime minister, who visited Motherwell this week to promote regional devolution within Scotland and drew on his experience as mayor of Greater Manchester.Again, without mentioning Andy Burnham by name, the first minister said: "Some think we should just be like Manchester. Well, I'm afraid I disagree."Scotland is no city. We are no region. We are a nation and soon we will be an independent nation."That went down well in the conference hall - even if the first minister is perfectly prepared to work with the prime minister on plans to create a regional level of government in Scotland, with powers transferred from both Westminster and Holyrood.Swinney also claimed that independence is "very close" in the full knowledge that there will not be another referendum unless there is a sustained surge in public support for Scottish statehood.Pledges on buses and misogynyPart of his strategy for achieving that is to demonstrate delivery in devolved government on issues of everyday concern.That's why he highlighted the roll out of the Scottish government's £2 bus fare cap as an example of cost of living support.It is already in place in the Highlands and across west central Scotland, and now he has confirmed its extension across north east Scotland from April.It should be available everywhere in Scotland by the end of this parliamentary term, by which time he said the Scottish government would, through franchising and regulation, have taken the bus network under public control.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, John Swinney, pictured with his son Matthew and wife, Elizabeth Quigley, at the SNP conference Announcements on making misogyny a specific criminal offence and new funding for community groups to fight racism are also designed to demonstrate a sense of immediate purpose.His speech seemed to energise those in the hall who are already with him. He also hopes it will engage those across Scotland who might be open to considering independence.Earlier this week, Swinney told me he is loving being first minister and intends to lead the SNP into the next Scottish Parliament election in 2031.However long he stays in office, this will always be a special conference for him - his first since leading his party through a successful Holyrood campaign and the one where he put the personal into his political commitment to independence.

schema.headline: Swinney's emotional explanation for his commitment to independence
